opus-5.5.text:
So what I mean is that the core recipe we developed for quadrupeds carries over surprisingly well to humanoids. When we started working on legged locomotion with reinforcement learning, a lot of the effort went into figuring out the pipeline: how do you set up massively parallel simulation on the GPU, how do you design rewards so the robot learns a natural, robust gait, how do you randomize the dynamics and the terrain so the policy doesn't overfit to the simulator, and how do you structure the curriculum so the robot gradually learns to handle stairs, slopes, rough ground, and so on.

What we found is that almost none of that is really specific to having four legs. The physics engine doesn't care, the PPO training loop doesn't care, the domain randomization ideas still apply, and the terrain curriculum works the same way. When you move to a humanoid, you swap in a different robot model, you adjust some reward terms, maybe you add things that matter more for bipeds like foot placement, keeping the torso upright, or arm swing, and you tune the observation and action spaces. But the overall framework, and a lot of the intuition about what makes sim-to-real work, transfers almost directly.

To be clear, it's not that a trained quadruped policy runs on a humanoid. Humanoids are harder in some ways: they're less statically stable, they have a smaller support polygon, and they fall more easily, so you have to be more careful about robustness and safety. The transfer is at the level of methodology. And that's a big part of why humanoid locomotion has progressed so quickly in the last couple of years. The community had already solved many of the hard problems on quadrupeds, so when good humanoid hardware became available, people could apply that toolbox right away instead of starting from scratch.

r001.rationale: It says the transfer is at the level of methodology, including shared training, randomization, and curriculum techniques.

r002.rationale: It clarifies that a trained quadruped policy does not run on a humanoid, but does not explicitly state that the humanoid policy must be retrained.

r003.rationale: It says to swap in a different robot model, but does not mention replacing a URDF file or state that the simulation pipeline accommodates this via that replacement.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So when I talk about transfer, I don't mean we take a policy trained on a quadruped and literally run it on a humanoid. The morphologies are too different for that to work. What transfers is the whole recipe for learning the controller.

When we started with ANYmal, the big question was whether you could learn a robust walking policy entirely in simulation with reinforcement learning and then deploy it on hardware without any fine-tuning. The pieces that made that work were things like massively parallel simulation, where you're running thousands of robots at once on a GPU so you get years of experience in hours. Then there's the curriculum over terrain difficulty, so the robot starts on flat ground and gradually sees stairs, slopes, gaps. There's domain randomization over masses, friction, motor delays, so the policy doesn't overfit to the simulator. And there's careful reward shaping, where you penalize things like joint torques and action rates so the gait is actually something the hardware can survive.

What we found is that almost none of that is specific to four legs. The reward terms are nearly identical. The randomization strategy is the same. The observation structure, proprioception plus commands plus some terrain information, is the same. So when we moved to a humanoid, the main work was swapping in the new robot model and dealing with the parts that really are different: the balance problem is harder because you have a much smaller support polygon, the upper body adds degrees of freedom you have to decide what to do with, and the failure modes are more dramatic because a fall from standing height is a bigger deal.

But the core loop, train in sim at scale, randomize, deploy, that carried over almost directly. Honestly, that was the surprising thing to me. I expected the humanoid to need a lot more hand-crafted structure, maybe some model-based component for balance. And it turned out that if the learning pipeline is set up well, the policy just figures out the balancing on its own, the same way the quadruped figured out how to recover from slips.

So "transfer" for me is really about the methodology being robot-agnostic, which is a much stronger claim than any particular policy being reusable.

r001.rationale: The response says the transferable contribution is the robot-agnostic learning methodology and pipeline, rather than the quadruped policy itself.

r002.rationale: It says the quadruped policy cannot simply run on the humanoid, then describes training and deploying a policy for the new robot using the carried-over pipeline.

r003.rationale: It mentions swapping in the new robot model, but does not specify replacing the robot’s URDF file.

astra-6.text:
What transfers is mostly the methodology, rather than the actual policy. You don’t take a controller trained for a quadruped and put it directly on a humanoid. But you can use the same reinforcement learning approach: train in simulation, give the robot an objective, like following a commanded velocity, and let it learn how to coordinate its joints.

For a humanoid, you change the robot model and adapt the rewards and constraints. Balancing on two legs introduces different challenges, and falls become a bigger concern. But much of the training machinery, including how you make the policy robust enough to transfer from simulation to hardware, carries over. So you’re building on the same framework rather than starting from scratch.

r001.rationale: It says the methodology and reinforcement-learning approach transfer, rather than the actual policy.

r002.rationale: It says a quadruped controller cannot be used directly on a humanoid and describes training the humanoid to learn its coordination.

r003.rationale: It mentions changing the robot model, but does not state that a general simulation pipeline accommodates the new robot by replacing its URDF file.

sol-6.1.text:
What transfers is really the learning approach, rather than a particular walking policy. With a quadruped, we train a policy in simulation that takes information about the robot—its joint positions, velocities, orientation, and the desired motion—and produces joint commands. We can use that same basic framework for a humanoid.

Of course, the robot is different, so we have to adapt the observations, the actions, and the reward. A humanoid has a smaller support area and has to balance on two legs, so you can’t simply take a quadruped policy and put it on a humanoid. But the tools for training, randomizing the simulation, and making the policy robust enough to run on hardware carry over. That means we don’t have to develop an entirely new locomotion controller from scratch for every robot.

r001.rationale: It says the learning approach and training tools transfer, rather than a particular walking policy.

r002.rationale: It says the framework must adapt to the humanoid and that the quadruped policy cannot simply be reused, but does not clearly state that the locomotion policy must be retrained.

r003.rationale: It does not mention a simulation pipeline accommodating a new robot by replacing its URDF file.
